Some people seem to believe that gender correction is about waking up the night after a drag show and calling to schedule surgery the day after. The process is of course not the same in every country, but I believe it shouldn't be vastly different (except for the fact that some countries still require sterilization before gender correction surgery). This is roughly the process is in an European country.

The first year, no transition is made at all. The first year is all about investigation in the social & psychological situation of the person in question, psychological tests, health check-ups, etc. The only treatment that can be given during this year is support from a therapist or similar. No diagnose is given at this point.

The second year, some treatment is initiated, but there are still much investigative moments left in the process. For example the person is expected to start living like he or she will be living after the transition. This is often before any hormone treatment or similar is given. When a specialized team of doctors and psychologists consider it likely that the person in question will actually transition, hormone treatment is initiated, together with speech therapy and body hair removal (for male-to-female). After this, the patient is "diagnosed" with being transgender.

After two years, it's possible to apply for a legal gender change and permission from state authorities to go through with gender correction surgery. Note that it's only possible to apply for permission, not that surgery will instantly be granted. No earlier than two and a half years, the legal gender can be changed. And no earlier than three years, the patient can undergo the first correctional surgery. Transitioning completely probably takes a lot longer than that. Oh, and you also have to be 18.

Worse than Highlander End Game? Worse than the live action adaptation of The Last Airbender? What about Superman IV? I respectfully disagree.

I feel that they did explain the backstories of the characters while remaining truthful to the source material. Honestly, Hellboys' background is explained just as well as it was in the graphic novel. While the deeper backstory of his birth is not detailed, it wasn't well delivered in the graphic novels either. However, the major points of the character were definitely hit upon. The evil act which summoned him and his transformation into an anti-hero for the forces of good were well done. His childlike demeanor emphasizes his forced isolation within the Bureau, which leads to interesting repercussions when he is allowed outside on missions.

Bruttenholms' pre-Hellboy experiences are not explored in depth but they aren't necessary considering it is presented that he is an academic who is known for an interest in the supernatural, hence his importance in the mission during 1944. His death came much earlier in the graphic novels than it did in the movie but we are none-the-less left with the knowledge that Bruttenholms' love for Hellboy is absolute as one would love their child. This gives the character a distinctive "father figure" background which was well established by the interaction between Hellboy and Bruttenholm.

Now, Abe Sapiens' background is light, granted, but it isn't widely explored in the beginning of the graphic novel. Not to mention that the movie is in-fact titled Hellboy and not "The Bureau of Paranormal Research and Defense". As such, Abes' place is to serve as a reasonable foil to Hellboy. In the sequel, we do learn more about Abe but in the first movie his experiences are not central to the plot other than to show that Hellboy is not alone in his isolation and his unusual nature in comparison to mankind.

Liz Shermans' backstory is established as a pyrokinetic with a troubled youth which makes sense that this leads to her being institutionalized due to stress and fear of a relapse in which she loses control of her powers. Being human, she has the added benefit of being able to leave The Bureau but it is painfully obvious that this is in some ways a curse when observing her relationship with Hellboy. Hellboy cannot be accepted by society while Liz can manage to exist among other humans. The inner turmoil presented by her powers is a dynamic struggle between the world of the supernatural and that of the regular. She serves as Hellboys connection to humanity after Bruttenholms' death. This establishes the romantic subplot to the movie.

Now, Rasputin was fairly obvious. Playing off of the historical knowledge that The Mad Monk was a "mystical" and "magical" holy man, the movie establishes that he has a significant position within Nazi Germany as the leader of an occult research group. The assassins aren't given more of a backstory but to be honest, they aren't given much of one in the graphic novel. They don't require a 30 minute exposition to establish that they are freaky badasses in the service of the Nazis.

To each his own, I suppose. Personally, I liked the movies and they were well received by the majority. On the other hand, Battlefield Earth was a wreck that nobody liked. Hellboy combined action, romance, and comedy in a lovely package, IMHO. The managing of several unusual character backgrounds was well handled in my opinion. The sequel was acknowledged for further delving into the supernatural underbelly which writhed beneath our visible world. The story of the Elves was well explained and served as an excellent point of motivation for the antagonists' actions against humanity.
